ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is bleeding from the genital tract after 20 weeks gestation but before delivery. It signals placental problems or trauma and requires rapid assessment to protect mother and fetus.

sections.p: Bleeding from the maternal genital tract after 20 weeks gestation, confirmed by visualisation of blood and exclusion of vaginal lesions.
b: Diagnosis is clinical; confirm gestational age and rule out lower genital tract sources.

t.b: Is the bleeding antepartum? Confirms timing and excludes miscarriage before 20 weeks.
Is the placenta anterior, posterior, or low‑lying? Detects placenta previa, abruption, or fetal distress.

b: Mild: stable vitals, no fetal compromise. Moderate: tachycardia, hemoglobin drop, possible fetal tachycardia. Severe: hypotension, shock, fetal bradycardia.

sections.p: Most APH arises from placental pathology, then trauma or coagulopathy.
b: Placenta previa (low‑lying placenta) – most common cause worldwide.
Vasa previa – fetal vessels over cervical os, high mortality if missed.
Placental abruption – abrupt separation, often with pain and uterine tenderness.
Uterine rupture – rare, usually in scarred uterus.
Infections (malaria, TB, HIV‑related thrombocytopenia) can precipitate bleeding.

sections.p: Bleeding may be painless (previa) or painful with uterine tenderness (abruption). Volume varies; fetal heart rate changes give clues.
b: Painless bright red bleeding → think previa.
Painful, clotted bleeding + rigid uterus → think abruption.
Bleeding after trauma or intercourse → consider laceration or vasa previa.

sections.p: Focused tests answer key questions about source, maternal status, and fetal wellbeing.

t.b: Where is the placenta? Detects previa, low‑lying cord, or abruption signs.
Is the fetus stressed? Decelerations suggest severe bleed or abruption.
Is the mother anemic or thrombocytopenic? Guides transfusion need.
Is disseminated intravascular coagulation present? Low fibrinogen signals severe abruption.
Is compatible blood ready? Essential before major transfusion.

sections.p: Rapid blood loss, maternal shock, and fetal distress are emergencies.
b: Maternal hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status.
Fetal bradycardia or absent variability.
Coagulopathy, DIC.

sections.p: Stabilise mother, treat cause, and plan delivery based on gestation and severity.
b: IV crystalloids and blood products to maintain MAP >65 mmHg.
Uterotonics (oxytocin) if atony contributes; avoid methylergometrine in hypertension.
For placenta previa: pelvic rest, tocolysis if pre‑term, and cesarean at 36‑37 weeks or earlier if unstable.
For abruption: maternal resuscitation, consider emergency delivery if fetal distress or severe bleed.

sections.p: After stabilisation, monitor hemoglobin, fetal growth, and counsel on risk reduction.
b: Repeat ultrasound to confirm placental position.
Avoid smoking, cocaine, and unprotected intercourse in late pregnancy.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic APH must be distinguished to avoid wrong management.
b: Vaginal lacerations – usually localized, not associated with placental location.
Hemorrhoids or rectal bleeding – dark, not bright red, and no uterine changes.
Uterine fibroid degeneration – pain dominant, bleeding usually post‑menstrual.

sections.p: Some investigations may appear normal despite serious pathology.
b: Ultrasound may miss a marginal previa if placenta migrates later; repeat later.
Normal coagulation tests early in abruption can rapidly deteriorate; repeat if bleeding continues.
Fetal heart rate may be temporarily normal in early abruption; continuous monitoring required.

whenToSeekHelp: Maternal blood pressure <90/60 mmHg, heart rate >120 bpm, or loss of consciousness.
Fetal heart rate <110 bpm or absent variability.

faq.a: The placenta lies over the cervical os, so when it separates it releases blood without uterine contraction.

faq.q: Can a small amount of bleeding be ignored?
faq.a: Even minor bleeding warrants evaluation because it may herald a serious underlying placental problem.

faq.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid?
faq.a: It inhibits fibrinolysis, reducing blood loss when given early in obstetric haemorrhage.

exam: Describe the clinical differences between placenta previa and placental abruption.
Explain the WHO grading of antepartum haemorrhage and its impact on management decisions.
List the immediate maternal and fetal investigations required when a pregnant woman presents with bleeding after 20 weeks.
